reigns_index.h: 1995 (circa) · AAWC (All Action, 1993)"Mr. Magnificent" Tom Adler — AAWC Universal Heavyweight Championship until 1995-11 (month) (Won the AAWC Universal Heavyweight title at the AAWC's own WrestleFest, beating the fed's own President Robert E. Schmid on the same card.) Defended on 5 August 1995 at Cameron Indoor Arena in a steel cage against GUNS, with GUNS' own Enterprises World Heavyweight Championship also at stake: Adler retained the Universal title and took the EN title as well, escaping over the cage while Hornet held GUNS off the arena floor on his shoulders. See this wing's own tier_source. A CSWA retrospective describes WrestleFest '95 differently: "the creation of an AAWC Universal Champion, merging the AAWC World Title with the AAWC Unified Title... The event featured GUNS, Hornet, Doctor Silver and Flic Rair. The first man to defeat his three opponents in consecutive matches would become the new champion" (promotions/cswa/archive/cswa-spotlight-hornet-vs-guns-1998.html), and does not name Adler among the four. The AAWC's own card of 5 August 1995 shows Adler as the reigning Universal Champion and replays his WrestleFest celebration. Both receipts are recorded; neither is picked over the other.

reigns_index.h: 1995 (year) · CSWA (1988)Mark Windham — United States Heavyweight Championship until 1995 (year) Its receipts are the Decatur card's report that Timmy "defeated Mark in the Windham Triangle Match" for the belt, that same broadcast calling him "the FORMER USN Champion" minutes later, and his own words at SHOWTIME at the Meadowlands of 17 January 1996: "I was the USN champion, ready.willing.and deserving of a shot at Steven Flair!" It is corroborated by two counts the fed keeps of him: FISH FUND XI of 6 September 1996 says the belt "is one that Mark Windham has held on at least four separate occasions", and CSWA PRIMETIME in New Orleans of 27 April 1997 bills him "a former four-time United States Heavyweight Champion" — four only if this reign is counted alongside the three the chain already carried. Neither the card he won it on nor the one he lost it on is held; the Thanksgiving Weekend Spectacular that ended it is named but not served.

12 July 1996 · CSWA (1988)Scotty Michaels — United States Heavyweight Championship won at BATTLE OF THE BELTS XIV until 1996 (year) (leg drop off the middle rope after Teri Melton hit Reno with a Top Rope DDT) This row previously ran to 1997-04-28, straight into Julius Godreign's reign. The fed's own FISH FUND XI of 6 September 1996 refutes it: Tom Adler is billed there as "the current USN Heavyweight Champion", has already taken the belt from Michaels and painted the AAWC's logo on it, and retains it against Mark Windham in a steel cage on night two.
Sources disagreeSources disagree INSIDE ONE DOCUMENT, resolved by the fed's own later text and recorded rather than quietly dropped. BATTLE OF THE BELTS XIV's own match call has Aaron Reno defending against Michaels, Teri Melton hitting Reno with a Top Rope DDT, and Michaels finishing with a leg drop off the middle rope: "ONE....TWO....THREE!! WE'VE GOT A NEW USN HEAVYWEIGHT CHAMPION!!" But that same card's closing recap, written in a different broadcast voice, runs through the night's title changes and calls one of them "a new USN Heavyweight Champion in Aaron Reno" — naming the man who LOST the belt. The registry follows the match call, because the fed's own FISH FUND XI of 6 September 1996 says outright that "Tom Adler took the title from Scotty Michaels", which only holds if Michaels left BATTLE OF THE BELTS XIV as champion. The recap's own words are preserved here.

CORRECTS the ledger's own compiled entry, which conflates two separate things under one wrong label. "Continental Connection" is the five-man STABLE Johnson and Bowman belonged to (with Stonebreaker, Bryson and Studd) — not this tag team's own name, which the broadcasts always give as "the Allies." reigns_index.h: 4 November 1997 · WWO (1995)"Prime Time" Phill Massacre — WWO International People's Championship end unknown (Awarded the restored WWO International People's Championship by the on-air WWO president character after "Ravashing" Ric Studd failed to appear for their scheduled title match (cited contractual obligations outside the WWO) — not a contested title change. Massacre had separately, moments earlier in the same segment, dropped his own WWO Extreme Championship to the mat unprompted.) CORRECTS the ledger's compiled note. The primary broadcast, read cover to cover, shows Studd was a no-show for the announced IP title match; the WWO's on-air president character declares Massacre "the official winner of this match" and hands him the newly-restored IP belt by decree — not by pinning or submitting Studd, who never appears in the segment at all. In the SAME ring segment, Massacre separately relinquishes his own WWO Extreme Championship, framed in his own words as personal ("I need to get rid of something, not only as a conscience..."), immediately after signing a new WWO contract — no narration ties the vacating of the Extreme title to the awarding of the IP belt as one "unification" transaction; they are two adjacent beats in the same segment, not one bout deciding both belts. This leaves the WWO Extreme Championship VACANT as of this date, a fact not reflected anywhere in the currently-held Extreme title reigns — NOT corrected here.

reigns_index.h: 1997 (year) · WWO (1995)Andros — WWO United States Championship end unknown (Defeated King $$$ Perfect.) The ledger gives no location. This reign (Andros over King $$$ Perfect) cannot be the same reign a 26 May 1997 broadcast (msg_id ylIv784kiMwJ) reports Andros reclaiming. This note narrows r003's own window. It does not change r003's won.date, which stays year-precision. The tournament's own semifinals and final were held the same night, at Battle of the Titans IV (18 Apr 1997). Underground Kingpin beat "Terrible" Travis Lee in one semifinal, Andros beat Jack "Tower of Terror" Harper in the other (msg_id dcyEFh4s03UJ, read cover to cover), and Kingpin then beat Andros in the final for the vacant title itself. This means r003's own 'Andros defeated King $$$ Perfect' bout, whatever its date, is very likely an EARLIER round of this SAME tournament, not a genuine championship reign. Andros never held the belt as champion at all under this reading. He reached the final and lost it there. r003's won.date can honestly be stated only as 'sometime in the Jan-Apr 1997 tournament window,' and its status as a 'reign' (rather than a bracket-advancement record inherited uncritically from the fed's own imprecise title-history ledger) is now in real doubt. Flagged as a structural question for the dedicated WWO reconciliation pass, not resolved by this patch.

reigns_index.h: 9 January 1998 · WWA (1997–2019)The Executive and Mr. Business — WWA World Tag Team Championship won at WWA — 9 Jan 1998 until 6 February 1998 (The Executives Club (Outlaw and The Executive) wins a four corners tournament match to become the first WWA Tag Team Champs.) Sources disagree on the pairing. WWA's own title history names the first champions as the Outlaw and The Executive. WWA's own served card of 9 January 1998 (wwa-1997-01-09, promotions/wwa/archive/1997-01-09.html) bills the belt as the CWC Northeast Tag Team Championship and has The Executive and Mr. Business win it: the pair come through a four-corners first round, then pin Triple Threat in the tournament's final, and the commentary calls them "the new and first Northeast Tag Champions"; the Outlaw hosts the night's Saloon segment and does not wrestle in the tournament. The cards of 14 January and 6 February 1998 also bring The Executive and Mr. Business out as the champions, and the card of 6 February 1998 (wwa-1998-02-06) has them lose the belts to the Commandant's Own. Both readings are recorded. The pair is filed as its own tag team, The Executive and Mr. Business (the-executive-and-mr-business-wwa), the Executive's Club being the stable they belong to (the-executives-club-wwa): the card of 9 January 1998 bills them "the Executive and Mr. Business of the Executive's Club" and the card of 14 January 1998, where they retain the belts over Matt Sanders and Canuck (Mr. Business pins Canuck with the Claw), brings them out "with their tag belts strung over their shoulders"; WWA's own title history carries the reign under the club's name.

reigns_index.h: 27 March 1998 · WWA (1997–2019)“Overlords of the Dark” — Darken & Steihl — WWA World Tag Team Championship won at Friday Night Fights — 27 Mar 1998 until 19 June 1998 (The heavy favorites going in, the Overlords do not disappoint and win the tournament.) WWA's own served card of 27 March 1998 (wwa-1998-03-20, promotions/wwa/archive/1998-03-20.html) puts the CWC Northeastern tag belts on the line and has the Overlords of the Dark (Darken and Steihl) beat House of Pain's Randy Cross and the Outlaw with a top-rope elbow from Darken. The belts had been declared vacant on the card of 27 February 1998 (wwa-1998-02-27), and the tournament for them opened on 13 March 1998 (wwa-1998-03-13), where Cross and the Outlaw won a first-round match; the card of 27 March does not itself call the match the tournament's final.

reigns_index.h: 17 December 1999 · UGA (1996)Disturbed Youth — WWC World Heavyweight Championship until 31 December 1999 (Won the first-ever WWC World Title change in Canada, in the first-ever three-way dance among the Sex and Violence trio (Stud/Kelly/Youth).) The 17TH WWC World Champion, per the fed's own title-history page's own numbering. The page's own blow-by-blow line for this reign ("Kelly pinned Stud thirty one minutes into the match to become the new champion") CONTRADICTS its own header crediting Disturbed Youth — an inconsistency preserved verbatim in the served document, not silently corrected. Recorded here under the header's own credited champion (Disturbed Youth), on two pieces of corroborating evidence inside the same document: the same entry's own "it was Youth's first World Title win" line, and the very next (18th) reign's own text, which has Shane Stud regaining the title specifically from "his Sex and Violence friend and partner Disturbed Youth" — confirming Youth, not Kelly, held it entering that match. The full transcript of that next match (promotions/uga/archive/carnacage-8.html) independently and unambiguously bills Disturbed Youth as the defending champion throughout, settling the question from a second served document.

reigns_index.h: 9 March 2001 · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)The Chef — European Championship won at Fusion 25 until 8 April 2001 The only PCW European Champion — he won it in the belt's own first match, a four corners against Hans Kruger, Slade and Chris Metal, and the reign ends with the belt retired under him rather than lost. The belt was announced at March Madness 2001 of 4 Mar 2001, where Hans Kruger challenged for "the first ever PCW European Title Match" on the strength of PCW's new European television deal, and created at Turmoil 26 of 6 Mar 2001 in the fed's own voice. Fusion 25 of 9 Mar 2001 crowned The Chef in a four corners match — "Clay Clayborne: The following contest is a four corners match for the PCW European Championship!" … "Winner and European Champion: The Chef Time: 9:56" … "So Chef is PCW's first European Champion" — and Sabotage 1 of 11 Mar 2001 corroborates it ("We see Chef win his match to become the first ever PCW European champion"). Two defences survive: Fusion 26 of 16 Mar 2001 ("Winner and still Euro Champion: The Chef Time: 7:15") and Turmoil 26 of 20 Mar 2001, a no-DQ falls-count-anywhere four corners the champion restipulated himself ("Winner and still European Champion: The Chef Time: 5:01"). Sabotage 3 of 25 Mar 2001 ran a seventeen-man battle royal for the number-one contendership, won by "The Graduate" Jay Gavin, and Spring Fling 2001 of 8 Apr 2001 is that title match — The Chef retained ("Winner: The Chef Time: 3:00") and the belt was retired in the same segment. Back to Old School 2001 of 16 Sep 2001 still bills him "PCW European champion" in his own ring introduction, among his other titles.

reigns_index.h: 13 March 2001 · FAW (2001)HaHaKlown — FAW World Heavyweight Championship won at Tuesday Torture until 11 May 2001 (The first FAW World Champion. The fed's own record says he was never beaten for the belt: he held it for roughly three months and handed it to his own sidekick Deadman before becoming president.) No date survives for either end of this reign; both edges are honestly unknown. Upgraded to an exact date on direct read of the deciding match itself: a three-fall (Hell in a Cell Street Fight / Submission / Buried Alive) encounter with Dogg, won 2 falls to 1, aided by an errant Olympian interference. FAW's own later recap (faw-is-war-2001-04-30.html) describes a brief interruption at Extreme Beating (2001-03) — HaHaKlown was made a co-champion with Sean Mason after a Laughing Scaffolding match neither man could actually lose — before "HaHaKlown won back his title the next show"; the fed's own retrospective frames the overall run as an unbroken ~3-month reign never lost in a straight fall, so that blip is recorded here rather than split into separate reign rows. Lost/ended 11 May 2001 (Panic), not by a pinfall but by retiring from in-ring competition to become FAW's third on-screen co-president alongside Bill Clinton and Sadam Hussain; Deadman is crowned new champion by acclamation the same night after his own separate hardcore-match win, not by beating HaHaKlown for the belt.

reigns_index.s: rising star championship | pcw (primetime, 2000–2004) | nikita morozov |  | nikita morozov
reigns_index.h: 20 July 2001 · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Nikita Morozov — Rising Star Championship won at Fusion 43 until 9 August 2001 Sources disagree — Turmoil 43, 14 Aug 2001 — five days after Dawning 2001 declared the belt vacant, the Turmoil strand still bills Nikita Morozov the champion and has him retain: "WINNER and still PCW Rising Star Champion: Nikita Morozov" (PCW's own results page for Turmoil 43, 14 Aug 2001). Turmoil 44 of 22 Aug 2001 then agrees with Dawning and runs a tournament for the vacated belt. Both show records stand; the reigns here follow Dawning 2001 and Turmoil 44, which agree with each other and with the fed's own next crowning. Fusion 43, 20 Jul 2001 — the show's own text crowns Nikita Morozov ("Winner and NEW Rising Star Champion"), and Snow is called "the former Rising Star champ" later on the same page. The card bills Morozov "(c)" and the fed's own log stores him as champion on both sides; the page's own crowning governs. No correction is filed on the stored champion-before: the fed's record carries no Rising Star row between Turmoil 37 of 12 Jun 2001 and this match, so who held the belt going in is not established beyond Snow's own last billing. Sabotage 13, 22 Jul 2001 — a NUMBER ONE CONTENDER'S cage match, not a title match, and the champion was not in it. The show says so in its own voice — "BJ Mac could become the number one contender for the Rising Star Title right here!" (PCW's own results page for Sabotage 13, 22 Jul 2001) — Clay announces only "here is your winner…BJ Mac!", and PCW's own results page for Dawning 2001, 9 Aug 2001 then says "BJ Mac has the right to challenge for the Rising Star Title" and introduces "the PCW Rising Star Champion......NIKITA MOROZOV". BJ Mac never held the belt, and Nikita Morozov's reign runs unbroken through this match. Dawning 2001, 9 Aug 2001 — Nikita Morozov defended the belt against BJ Mac and kept it ("WINNER: Nikita Morozov, TIME: 9:28"), and the fed took it off him in the same breath: "Unfortunately for Morozov, this defense is said to be his last. Due to a rule violation, Morozov is no longer allowed to hold the Rising Star Title and it is now vacant" (PCW's own results page for Dawning 2001, 9 Aug 2001). PCW's own results page for Turmoil 44, 22 Aug 2001 confirms it from the other side — a tournament "for the vacated PCW Rising Star Title", with Morozov called "the now former Rising Star champion" who "retained the Rising Star title until he was forced to relinquish it".

reigns_index.s: women's championship | gcw (gcwonline.net) | icebabe |  | icebabe
reigns_index.h: 2001-08-08 (circa) · GCW (gcwonline.net)Icebabe — Women's Championship won at Meltdown 21 until between 2001-08-08 and 2001-08-23 (circa) Sources disagree — the fed's own Meltdown 24 bills Gidget the champion and its stored booking date is 2001-07-10, but the same card's own text recaps 'Heatwave' in the past tense ("At Heatwave last Sunday, the armies of GCW defeated those of the ACWF and CWU…") and both the World and TV title histories date Heatwave to 2001-08-20, six weeks after that booking date. The women's title cards are therefore dated by the fed's own Meltdown archive list (Meltdown 21 circa 8 Aug 2001, Meltdown 24 circa 23 Aug 2001, Meltdown 33 circa 8 Nov 2001) rather than by their stored booking dates. The first GCW Women's Championship, won in a five-way battle royal. Andrews: "Here is your winner, and the first GCW Women's champion… Icebabe!" Moments after the announcement the other four entrants (billed collectively in the same text as 'the Cherry Bombs') powerbomb her; the text stages this as a beatdown, never a title change ("Icebabe, the women's champion, has been laid out by the Cherry Bombs!"). The fed's own roster has no page for this holder.

reigns_index.h: 30 September 2001 · GCW (gcwonline.net)Octavian — World Heavyweight Championship won at FallOut 2001 until 23 December 2001 The page's own Reign cell reads '84 days'. The fed's own card of Meltdown 38 (13 Oct 2001), dated inside this reign's own window: Toad pinned Octavian clean for the belt after Jason Dread's ringside chair shot -- meant for Toad -- struck Octavian instead (“Toad gets to the top, and measures Octavian! Here it comes… TOAD JAM! HE HITS IT!… Toad hooks the leg! ONE! TWO! THREE!!!”, followed a few lines later by “Toad rolls over and hooks Octavian’s leg! Dread is out of sight! The referee counts! ONE!! TWO!!! THREE!!!!!”, and Andrews announcing Toad “the NEW GCW World Heavyweight Champion”). Minutes later, Commissioner Mr. Danger reverses the decision from the ramp, on-air, after a MegaTron replay of Dread's chair shot: “if you look back at the tape, you’ll see that Jason Dread entered the ring and hit Octavian with a steel chair… in GCW, a title can only change hands via pinfall or submission… I fear I have no other choice, than to reverse the decision of this match… therefore, your winner, via disqualification… and STILL YOUR GCW World Heavyweight Champion… Octavian!” The belt is handed back to Octavian on the same broadcast; no reign changes hands and this reign's own won/lost dates and holder are unaffected.

reigns_index.h: between 2001-10-09 and 2001-10-12 (circa) · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Da Westsidaz — Tag Team Championship until 30 October 2001 Red October 2001, 21 Oct 2001 — Da Westsidaz are billed and retain as champions; the change back from the European Union is not in the fed's own record. THE TOURNAMENT IS THE VEHICLE, and it is a title tournament, not a contender tournament mis-titled: PCW calls it "the Tag Team Title Tournament" (Turmoil 49), "the PCW tag team title tournament" (Turmoil 49, Fusion 52), a "second round PCW Tag Team Title Tournament Match" (Turmoil 50), a "second round world tag team title tourney match" (Fusion 53) and a "third round match in the PCW tag team tournament" / "semi-final matchup in our PCW Tag Team Title Tourney" (Fusion 54), and no page ever calls any of it a number-one contenders match. Da Westsidaz went through it — first round Turmoil 49 of 26 Sep, second round Turmoil 50 of 2 Oct, semi-final Turmoil 51 of 9 Oct over the Golden Game — and emerge from it champions: by Fusion 54 of 12 Oct the fed bills the other semi-final as being for "a spot in the Tag Team title match at Red October against Da Westsidaz" and for "a shot at the tag belts at Red October", and at Red October Clay announces the match "for the PCW Tag Team Championship" and introduces them as "the PCW Tag Team Champions…DA WESTSIDAAAAAZZZZZ" with the card reading "Da Westsidaz (c)". A TAG RESULT IS NOT A TITLE CALL, so the win is bracketed 9–12 Oct rather than dated to the Turmoil 51 tourney match, which carries no title stipulation and no crowning. THE SECOND READING, recorded and not followed: that Red October is the tournament FINAL and the "(c)" is the card's own error, which would date the win 21 Oct 2001 exact. It is not followed because the fed's own ring announcer names them champions BEFORE the bell and Fusion 54 bills them champions nine days earlier, while nothing but the tournament's own name argues the other way; Dave's closing line is "DA WESTSIDAZ ARE THE FIVE TIME TAG TEAM CHAMPIONS", never "new". Sabotage 21 of 7 Oct 2001 agrees that the belt was not yet theirs: Da Westsidaz are in a four-team single-elimination TLC match with no title stipulation and nobody billed champion, and are eliminated by Kon Xeuhui. The change itself is in no surviving PCW page; the date is the bracket the fed's own record supports.

The earlier passes read PCW's own results page for Sabotage 26, 25 Nov 2001’s card ("Jeremy Howard vs Timo Bolamba (c)") as a Sunday Sabotage-strand instance, on the reasoning that Kramer Wild Wing had been champion since Red October 2001 and Timo Bolamba was PCW’s Rising Star champion. The Sunday Sabotage strand loses an instance on this belt. The log stores no champion change here and takes no correction — the row for the match does not exist at all.

reigns_index.s: rising star championship | pcw (primetime, 2000–2004) | el diablo |  | el diablo
reigns_index.h: 7 December 2001 · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)El Diablo — Rising Star Championship won at Fusion 62 until 9 January 2002 Sources disagree — Sabotage 28, 9 Dec 2001 — the Sabotage strand bills Gaijin the standing Rising Star Champion and crowns Orpheus Grant over him ("the Rising Star champion" inside the match; "Winner: Orpheus Grant"), two days after Fusion 62 of 7 Dec 2001 ended "Winner and NEW Rising Star Champion: El Diablo" and two days before Turmoil 60 bills "El Diablo (c)". No match on either strand returns the belt. The reigns here follow the Fusion/Turmoil strand. The same Sabotage 28 page also bills a third man, "the current PCW Rising Star Champion, “Big” Bubba McCoy … proudly clutching his belt". Sabotage 28, 9 Dec 2001 — Orpheus Grant won the match but the belt did not move on the Fusion/Turmoil strand; El Diablo is billed champion on Turmoil 60 two days later and retains on Sabotage 29 a fortnight after that. Turmoil 60, 11 Dec 2001 — a disqualification, and the champion kept the belt: the card reads "El Diablo (c) vs Big Bubba McCoy vs Gaijin" and the match ends "Winner via DQ: Gaijin" after El Diablo knocked Gaijin out with the ring bell ("What a load of bunk using a weapon to keep his title"). The fed's own log agrees — El Diablo before and after — and Sabotage 29 of 23 Dec 2001 ends "Winner and STILL PCW Rising Star Champion: El Diablo", with Sabotage 30 of 30 Dec and Sabotage 31 of 6 Jan 2002 billing him champion too. Turmoil 64, 8 Jan 2002 — a NUMBER ONE CONTENDER'S match, not a title match. The show announces it in its own voice: "This over the top rop battle royal will determine the # 1 contender for the Rising Star title", and the same show has El Diablo walk backstage "the Rising Star title around his waist". Hessian never held the belt; the stored champion-after is corrected. El Diablo held the belt through Sabotage 31 of 6 Jan 2002 (a four-way the referee ruled a non contest) and is shown with it backstage on Turmoil 64 of 8 Jan; the reign ends on the first of Shanghaied 2002's two Rising Star matches.

The outcome of that match is unattested in anything held, so the reign stays open at the end of the record rather than being closed on the booking.

a.title: unified world tag team championships | cswa-unified-world-tag-team

reigns_index.h: 2001 (year) · CSWA (1988)Simply Stunning — Unified World Tag Team Championships end unknown (the holders on the fed's own Champions page of April 2001, since PRIMETIME in Paducah) Three defenses are recovered from the fed's own 2001 cards, none of which moves the belts: a fifteen-minute time-limit draw against The Professionals at PRIMETIME in Tacoma on 6 October 2001, announced as a draw after the referee had already counted three for the champions; and the champions still billed and defending as of PRIMETIME in New Orleans (11 November) and PRIMETIME in St. Louis (26 December), where they challenge the whole tag division to a gauntlet match at ANNIVERSARY. A FOURTH defense, dated to the day, is the one that challenge was building to: the four-way HOUSE OF PAIN cage match at ANNIVERSARY 2001 on 31 December 2001, in which the champions RETAIN. Michael Hardy takes most of the match's punishment, is spike-tombstoned and busted open, and still scores both of his team's falls -- cradling WJ Mills out of a FrankenParsons to eliminate Raw Deal, then splashing both Professionals off the top of the cage on a Rocket Launcher from Simon Wilcox for the win, with the CS Express on the floor to stop Eddie Mayfield's chairshot first. The fed's own cards call this belt the Unified Tag Team Championships in their section headers and the CSWA World Tag Team Titles in their commentary, within the same document; both readings are recorded and neither is resolved. One of the champions puts the length of this reign at "six months or so" on 26 December 2001, which does not sit with the reign's own recorded start at PRIMETIME in Paducah in February 2001; that disagreement is recorded too. The ANNIVERSARY card adds a THIRD spelling to that first disagreement and resolves nothing: its own section header reads "the CSWA Unified Tag Team Titles" and its commentary "the Unified Tag Team Championships".

reigns_index.h: between 2002-01-09 and 2002-01-15 (circa) · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Brandi — Extreme Championship until between 2002-01-20 and 2002-02-01 (circa) Sources disagree — Shanghaied 2002 of 9 Jan 2002 crowns HANK~! Extreme Champion in its own voice ("HANK~! HAS DONE IT! HANK~! Has won the PCW Extreme Title!"), and six days later PCW's own results page for Turmoil 65, 15 Jan 2002 bills Brandi the champion and has her retain, as does PCW's own results page for Sabotage 33, 20 Jan 2002 — with no match returning the belt to her. Both show records stand. Turmoil 65, 15 Jan 2002 — the show has BRANDI retain, not HANK~! win: "Brandi is showing why she's the extreme champ" … "Brandi … hits Pure Exctasy on him and makes the cover" … "AND HANK~! JOBBED!!!! Returning everything in this universe back to normal." PCW booked the change on an OFF-PAGE SUNDAY SHOW. PCW's own results page for Sabotage 33, 20 Jan 2002 has Brandi retain against Corey Williams ("she is the current Extreme Champion, Brandi!") and announces the next one twice in its own voice — "they both have an Extreme Title match this Sunday with Hank~! and Big Daveylicious also involved" and "that four way Extreme Title match this Sunday at Shang-hied 2". PCW's own booking record carries no show on Sunday 27 Jan 2002 and no results page for one survives, so the four-way that made HANK~! champion was held on a show that left no page. The change itself is in no surviving PCW page; the date is the bracket the fed's own record supports.

reigns_index.s: continental championship | pcw (primetime, 2000–2004) | jeremy 'krayzie' howard |  | jeremy 'krayzie' howard
reigns_index.h: between 2002-02-22 and 2002-03-04 (circa) · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Jeremy 'Krayzie' Howard — Continental Championship until 7 April 2002 The bracket tightens twice: from 10 Feb – 4 Mar 2002 to 17 Feb – 4 Mar and now to 22 Feb – 4 Mar 2002 on PCW's own results page for Fusion 72, 22 Feb 2002, which brings Chet King out as "PCW Continental Champion" and has Howard call himself "the number one contender to his Continental title" on the same page. PCW ran two shows inside the tightened window — Sabotage 37 of 24 Feb and Turmoil 71 of 26 Feb 2002 — and neither page names a Continental champion or carries a Continental title match, so the change is unrecorded rather than uncollected; a results page survives for every show PCW’s own booking record carries in the window. The log stores Drake Maxwell as champion before and after the March Madness match; he is neither, and both values are corrected. Fusion 75, 23 Mar 2002 — a DOUBLE COUNT OUT, not a title change. The show's own page has Jeremy "Krayzie" Howard come out first WITH the belt and challenge the contender on the spot ("I'm challenging Kannon to a PCW Continental title match right NOW!", "Its about time he gave Kannon his rematch"), calls Howard "the Continental Champion" three times inside the match, and ends "WE HAVE A DOUBLE COUNT OUT! … They'll have to settle this thing at Spring Fling once and for all!" The card line "Xavier Kannon (c)" is contradicted by its own page and is a card-line error inside one document, not a second source. The fed's own log stores Kannon as champion before AND after; both values are corrected. Fusion 76 of 29 Mar 2002 carries a byte-for-byte copy of this match; it is the same match, not a rematch. Turmoil 76, 2 Apr 2002 — Howard defends the belt against The Chef ("PCW CONTINENTAL CHAMPION..... JEREMY HOWARD!!!!!", entering "with the Continental title slung over his shoulder"); the match breaks down under a chair attack and the fed's own log records no change. The reign runs unbroken from the February/March bracket to Spring Fling: the two reigns the log implied in between (a Kannon reign off Fusion 75 and a second Howard reign off Turmoil 76) rested on the Fusion 75 double count out and its Fusion 76 duplicate, and neither moved the belt. The change itself is in no surviving PCW page; the date is the bracket the fed's own record supports.

reigns_index.h: 2002-02 (circa) · PTC (2002)Vampir Nosferatu (PCW) — PTC Global Championship end unknown (Won a 128-competitor Global Title Contenders Tournament (80 signed in the first 72 hours); the deciding match went to Nosferatu 25–22 by fan vote, over Jay Phoenix. Styled on-screen as both “PTC Global Championship” and “Primetime Central Global Champion.”) From the Feb 2002 PTC relaunch. Holder is vampir-nosferatu-pcw: the GTT1 final was shown on PCW's Friday Fusion of 23 November 2001, whose served card carries the PCW record, and this reign's own label bills him PCW. The OSW record of the same name is the same man (PCW's own card and OSW's own roster card agree on Havana, Cuba, The Cuban Uprising and the entrance music), so the two records merge. TOURNAMENT FINAL AND DATE, TWO RECEIPTS THAT DISAGREE: the I-PPV site's own front page states "For the first time since Vampir Nosferatu defeated Jay Phoenix in late 2001, the PTC Global Title will finally find a home" — naming Jay Phoenix as the man beaten in that deciding match, and dating it to late 2001. This row's own won date, drawn from the alliance news engine, reads 2002-02. Both are recorded; neither is picked. Jay Phoenix was the runner-up in that final and never a champion of this belt. TIER-3: PTCpedia's own title-history article independently dates and stages the GTT1 final at PCW's Friday Fusion, 23 Nov 2001, matching the I-PPV site's own "late 2001" reading rather than the alliance news engine's "2002-02" — a second source now favors late 2001, though neither reading is struck per the standing sources-disagree rule. The same article gives the reason for the stripping this row's own holder never explained: Vampir "was later discovered to have used work written by another." PTCpedia's own PTC Global Title article (/promotions/ptc/archive/ptcpedia-ptc-global-title.html, captured 19 Aug 2010) — a fuller, later-compiled title history than the alliance news engine's own partial lineage; per docs/PROCESS.md's hub rule, its claims corroborate the existing record rather than override it.

reigns_index.h: 31 March 2002 · FAW (2001)The Omega Fro — FAW World Heavyweight Championship won at Extreme Beating II until 2002-04 (month) (Pinned champion Spawn with the Armageddon.) Open-ended as of this read. Tony Vigilante, who made the save, turns on Fro immediately after the bell. Lost the title at "Breaking Point," a 2002 pay-per-view booked in-storyline on Panic (12/27 April 2002, faw-panic-2002-04-12/27) and Hot Stuff (21 April 2002) as a Fatal Four-Way (Fro defending against Tony Vigilante, Ben Hart, and Spawn) -- no recap of that show survives in the held record. Tony Vigilante is confirmed the new champion by Distortion 6 (2002, faw-distortion-6-2002), read in full, which bills him as reigning champion entering its own Hell in a Cell main event. CORROBORATED (May Day Massacre, 2002-05, read in full): a recap video narrates this same title change in more detail -- Vigilante, aided by New School (Kyle Kilbane and Shawn Herrera), stripped Fro of the title at Breaking Point. FURTHER CORROBORATED (Panic, 3 May 2002, faw-panic-2002-05-03, read in full): a second replay segment shows the fuller Breaking Point sequence -- New School (Kyle Kilbane, Shawn Herrera) run in during a Fro/Ben Hart brawl also involving Spawn and Tony Vigilante, help Vigilante clear out Fro and Hart, then double-superkick and jackknife-powerbomb Spawn before Vigilante submits him with three chairs laid over the other three men, each reading "Justice Has Prevailed."

reigns_index.s: continental championship | pcw (primetime, 2000–2004) | xavier kannon |  | xavier kannon
reigns_index.h: 7 April 2002 · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Xavier Kannon — Continental Championship won at Spring Fling 2002 until 28 May 2002 Turmoil 78, 16 Apr 2002 — Kannon's first recorded defence, against Frisco ("Kannon defends the Continental title against Frisco", "Kannon loses the match, but not the Continental Title"). He is billed the standing champion on every surviving page of the stretch: Turmoil 77 of 10 Apr (results/495.txt, "PCW CONTINENTAL CHAMPION..... XAVIER KANNON!!!!!"), Sabotage 42 of 14 Apr (results/356.txt, "the current Continental Champion Xavier Kannon!"), Sabotage 43 of 21 Apr (results/357.txt) and Fusion 79 of 3 May (results/222.txt). Turmoil 84 of 18 Jun has Kannon himself date the reign in the fed's own voice — "Two months and twelve days since I won the Continental Title" — which lands on 19 Jun, one day off this show, corroborating the 7 Apr win. Sabotage 43, 21 Apr 2002 — Kannon defends against Legend Inc. and the Sabotage strand AGREES with the Turmoil/Fusion strand here ("the PCW Continental Champion…… XAVIER KANNON!!"), as Sabotage 42 of 14 Apr does. No Sabotage instance arises on this belt in this stretch. Fusion 79, 3 May 2002 — the "PCW LEGEND'S GAUNTLET MATCH OF DEATH", a gauntlet the CHAMPION worked through, ending "THE WINNER OF THIS MATCH......XAVIER KANNON!!!" The show's own page announces it in advance — "XAVIER KANNON WILL DEFEND HIS CONTINENTAL TITLE AGAINST A…SCARY…MYSTERY OPPONENT?" — and bills him "the Commissioner of PCW and the PCW Continental champion......GOLD PATRON MERITORIOUS XAVIER KANNON!". Scott Kilborn is the last of the gauntlet opponents; the card's trailing "(c)" sits on his name and the fed's own log takes him for the champion on both sides. Both values are corrected. Kannon then retains again at Supremacy 2002, 22 May 2002 (results/518.txt) — "the match to decide the PCW Continental Champion, the Champion Xavier Kannon against our very own Duke Williams", ending on Kannon's own three count — a defence the fed's own title log never recorded. The reign ends by the fed stripping him, not in a match, and the fed says so on both sides of it: Turmoil 84 of 18 Jun 2002 has Kannon protest "TWO MONTHS AND TWELVE DAYS since I won the Continental Title and did I ever lose it? Was I pinned for, or submitted for it? NO I WAS NOT!" while the same show books "a Triple Threat Match to determine the Number One Contender to the PCW Continental Championship" and calls him "the last Continental Champion"; Turmoil 85 of 3 Jul (results/503.txt) has him say "MY Continental Title.... WHICH I HAVE NOT BEEN PINNED FOR goes to Legend Inc." The immediately preceding log row, Turmoil 80 of 21 May 2002, is a REPLAYED TAPE, not a title change: its own text opens "Sunday Sabotage:September 2, 2001- Boda vs The Chef vs Howard Porter" and the show frames it as a retrospective ("we're gonna show Boda's greatest moment in The Red Army. That would be when he won the Continental title", "Boda's one and only Continental title reign lasted a little over three weeks"). The genuine match is Sabotage 17, Boda's September 2001 reign; the fed's own booking dates that show 3 Sep 2001 while the replay caption says 2 Sep 2001. Kannon defends the belt the night AFTER the replay, at Supremacy 2002 on 22 May 2002, which settles it.

reigns_index.s: cruiserweight championship | pcw (primetime, 2000–2004) | rent-a-hero |  | rent-a-hero
reigns_index.h: 7 April 2002 · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Rent-a-Hero — Cruiserweight Championship won at Spring Fling 2002 until 28 May 2002 Spring Fling 2002, 7 Apr 2002 — "WINNER OF THIS MATCH AND NEW CRUISER WEIGHT CHAMPION: RENT-A-HERO!" (PCW's own results page for Spring Fling 2002, 7 Apr 2002). Anton the Kid's reign runs 12 Mar – 7 Apr 2002 unbroken; the two matches inside it that the fed's log files as changes (Charlie Loc, THE Multiple Man) were a non-title match and a contendership match. Turmoil 77, 10 Apr 2002 — a DISQUALIFICATION, which does not move a belt: Juan Borro runs in and cracks Kramer Wild Wing with a chair, "The ref immediately calls for the bell. Winner via DQ: Kramer Wild Wing" (PCW's own results page for Turmoil 77, 10 Apr 2002). Rent-A-Hero is billed and defends as champion on both sides — Fusion 79 of 3 May ("Winner: Rent A Hero", PCW's own results page for Fusion 79, 3 May 2002) and Supremacy 2002 of 22 May ("he is the current PCW Cruiserweight Champion... Rent-A-Hero", PCW's own results page for Supremacy 2002, 22 May 2002) — and no match returns the belt to him. His reign is one unbroken run, 7 Apr – 28 May 2002. The card of Turmoil 81 bills "Kramer Wild Wing (c)"; that is a card-line error.

reigns_index.h: 21 April 2002 · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Snow — World Championship won at Sabotage 43 until 22 May 2002 Turmoil 80 of 21 May 2002 is a RETROSPECTIVE, and the World Championship battle royal filed on it is a replayed tape. The show is titled "Boda's PCW legacy in memoriam", runs a career retrospective in clips throughout, and frames this one in its own voice — "When we come back, Boda's first World title victory at March Madness", "Let's go to the tape" — with the tape's own slate reading "PCW March Madness:March 3, 2002- Battle Royal for the PCW World Heavyweight Title" (PCW's own results page for Turmoil 80, 21 May 2002). The genuine title change is March Madness 2002 — Boda's 4–6 Mar 2002 reign, which the retrospective itself corroborates ("that is when Boda captured the Heavyweight title"). Row 904 is dropped from the chain (the replay-document model, the museum's own rule; the row-873 / row-872 / row-903 precedent) with no correction row: the stored champions are correct for the match that actually happened, eleven weeks earlier. The next night's Supremacy 2002 card bills "Jason Snow (c)" and crowns Big Alan Steele over him. The tape's own slate dates March Madness 2002 to 3 March where his booking dates it to 4 March; the booking date governs. Turmoil 80's Continental half is likewise a replayed Sabotage 17 tape of Sep 2001.

reigns_index.s: hdtv championship | gcw (gcwonline.net) | the almighty kippo |  | the almighty kippo
reigns_index.h: 28 April 2002 · GCW (gcwonline.net)The Almighty Kippo — HDTV Championship won at Warpath 2002 until between 2002-05-26 and 2002-07-27 (circa) The page's own Reign cell reads '24 days'. The fed's own roster has no page for this holder. The card of Shockwave 2002 (26 May 2002) has him retain over Moraless ("Here is your winner and still GCW Television champion, the Almighty Kippo!"); at Dangerous Games 2002 (circa 27 Jul 2002) he is "The Almighty Kippo, former Television Champion", and Meltdown, Episode 61 (1 Aug 2002) books The Tyrant and LeStatt Knight "for the vacant GCW Television title". The fed's own Television Title History as captured on 21 April 2003 ends with this reign and lists the title Vacant. Sources disagree — the fed's later Television Title History page runs this reign on to Jonathan Borealis (6-2-05) and carries a reign after it, '13a | Moraless | Unknown | Unknown | 17 days'; no held card shows Moraless holding the title (he loses to this champion at Shockwave 2002 and is on no later 2002 card), the 2003 capture has no such reign, and the later page's own synopsis of reign 14 says the title went dark: "After years of inactivity, the TV title was ressurrected at Warpath 2005". The reign is recorded as ending with the title vacant between Shockwave 2002 and Dangerous Games 2002; no held card shows how it left him. The card of Warpath 2005 reintroduces the belt with no champion: President Caldera tells Capo, who has taken it, "YOU ARE NOT TELEVISION CHAMPION" and announces "we will be crowning the new Television Champion" in a battle royal, which WorldWide 15 (2 Jun 2005) holds without him.

reigns_index.s: united states championship | gcw (gcwonline.net) | toad |  | toad
reigns_index.h: 28 April 2002 · GCW (gcwonline.net)Toad — United States Championship won at Warpath 2002 until between 2002-06-06 and 2003-04-21 (circa) The page's own Reign cell reads '42 days'. The reign did not end in a match: the card of Meltdown, Episode 60 (circa 6 Jun 2002) has him retain, "He's the final Hardcore and United States champion!"; the fed's own news post (8 Nov 2008) names Toad 'the final title holder' when GCW closed in 2002 and records that he refused to return the belt and melted it down; the fed's own United States Title History as captured on 21 April 2003 lists the title Vacant. When GCW came back in 2005 the title was decided by a one-night, four-man tournament on WorldWide 3 (23 Feb 2005), in which NBK beat Toad in the semi-final; the page's next row (No. 11, LeStatt Knight, 2-23-05) is that tournament's winner, not a win over Toad. The staging survives only as a compilation copy: the Warpath card of 28 Apr 2002 holds the World title match alone, and the match this reign begins at survives as the fed's own card on the 2003 best-of DVD, billed 'Warpath, April 2002'.

reigns_index.h: 2002-04 (month) · FAW (2001)Tony Vigilante — FAW World Heavyweight Championship won at Breaking Point until 2002-05 (month) (Submits Spawn in a No-Disqualification Fatal Four Way at Breaking Point, with New School's interference -- the champion (The Omega Fro) did not have to be pinned under this match's own explicit rule.) The June 2002 snapshot has Vigilante as champion and the Hall of Fame has The British Bomber winning the belt at Diabolical Day that July, so this reign precedes r013 in calendar order. Both receipts are recorded rather than resequenced. UPDATE: Vigilante loses the title clean via submission (his own Justification, reversed) to Spawn in a four-way Hell in a Cell main event, undated beyond "2002" but placed four days before May Day Massacre. This is a primary-source read outranking the June 2002 champions-page snapshot that originally dated this reign, so it now supplies the reign's lost edge -- but it does NOT resolve the existing sources-order tension the predecessor flagged: that June snapshot still bills Vigilante as champion, meaning either he regained the title again before June (not yet corroborated anywhere in the held record) or the snapshot itself is simply wrong/stale. FURTHER UPDATE (May Day Massacre, 2002-05, read in full): this same show explicitly bills Vigilante as still-reigning champion (carrying the physical belt, addressed as champion) in its own six-man Old School vs New School main event -- directly contradicting the Distortion 6 loss recorded above, despite May Day Massacre airing chronologically after Distortion 6. Left unresolved -- a genuine fed-side continuity error between two shows, not a Museum reading error. CONFIRMED (Diabolical Day 2002, 21 July 2002, faw-diabolical-day-2002-2002-07-21, read in full): this show's own referee introduction explicitly describes Tony Vigilante holding "the Title he left vacant" as a prop while serving as special guest referee for the tournament final -- direct primary-source confirmation the title was vacant entering this show, corroborating this row's own closing note rather than resolving the still-open Distortion-6/May-Day-Massacre contradiction, which remains unaddressed.

reigns_index.s: syndicate championship | rush (2002) | statuz quo |  | statuz quo
reigns_index.h: 23 May 2002 · RUSH (2002)Statuz Quo — Syndicate Championship won at Adrenaline 4 until 18 August 2002 The champion renamed the belt, in character, for the length of his reign. On the card of Adrenaline 5 (30 May 2002) he announces it himself: "I deserve not da 'Syndicate title' but my own! Datz why I'm officially renamin' da title to da \"Quo title\" fo' as long as my reign as champion!!", with a custom platinum belt unveiled on camera and a champion-declared stipulation, "from now on, diz title will only be defended in no disqualification matches". He repeats it on Adrenaline 10: "I am the QUO CHAMPION!!". This is not a second belt and not a rename by the federation: the announce team calls it degrading the Syndicate title, the fed's own title list keeps the name Syndicate Championship, the page heads its list "Syndicate Championship", and the next champion's own words are "how long it took for El Spiffy! to get the Quo-stink off of the belt". Three defences are on held cards, none in the fed's own title log: Ignition 2002 (16 Jun 2002, beat Christopher Shackelton in a match announced "for one fall with no disqualifications and is for the Syndicate title", his own declared stipulation honoured), Adrenaline 8 (27 Jun 2002; he lost the match by disqualification and kept the belt, the card's words being "Winner by DQ: Steve Brent. Statuz Quo retains his Syndicate Title") and Adrenaline 11 (25 Jul 2002, beat Caleb McGlocklan by pinfall). A fourth match is explicitly not a title match: on Adrenaline 10 Sheila Tyrone introduces "a non-title match", which Statuz Quo lost to William 'Biohazard' Perry. The page's "Longest Title Holder: Statuz Quo-87 days" agrees exactly with 23 May to 18 August.

reigns_index.h: between 2002-05-31 and 2002-06-30 (circa) · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Reginald P. Lovecraft — Extreme Championship until 30 June 2002 No match putting the belt on Lovecraft survives, and the June 2002 stretch is recorded rather than modelled: Fusion 80 of 31 May 2002 ends "Winner and NEW EXTREME CHAMPION: MIYAGAWA!" and then has the belt taken off him in the same segment ("A ref comes over intending to hand the Extreme title to Miyagawa but Ellie snaps the belt off him"); PCW's own results page for Turmoil 82, 4 Jun 2002 calls Eleanor Hall "the new Extreme Champion" on the strength of that, and PCW's own results page for Turmoil 83, 11 Jun 2002 says the belt had been "swapp[ed]... between them and Ellie~!" over the preceding weeks. No reign is filed for Eleanor Hall — a belt taken with a baseball bat and one commentary line is the SOCIETY shape the tenth pass declined on the Cruiserweight belt — and Lovecraft rides a bracketed reign because the fed's own voice bills him the champion on the night he lost it and again three days later. The change itself is in no surviving PCW page; the date is the bracket the fed's own record supports. The reign is named twice from outside PCW, and neither source is PCW's own, so the grade stands unchanged: PTCpedia's own Politically Incorrect article (/promotions/ptc/archive/ptcpedia-politically-incorrect.html) says “Lovecraft himself gained a measure of revenge on Kannon, taking the PCW Extreme Title from the Scientologist”, and Sin City Championship Wrestling's own biography card for him lists “PCW Extreme Champion” among his honours. Both disagree with PCW's own pages about whom he took the belt from: PTCpedia names Xavier Kannon, where PCW has Miyagawa win it on 31 May 2002 and the belt swapped around Eleanor Hall through June, and no PCW page stages a Kannon–Lovecraft Extreme Title change. Both readings stand.

reigns_index.h: 16 June 2002 · PURE (2002)The HIT — PURE Jr. Heavyweight Title won at Ikusa V end unknown (Pinned The End after the Double Neurotica, in a tag match the fed put the champion's own title on — whoever pinned The End won the belt.) The fed's own complete Junior Heavyweight Championship history numbers him its second champion and names the win, in a six man tag team match, at a show it calls Ikusa III; the script that carries that bout is Ikusa V's, of 16 June 2002, and both stand. The fed's own earlier paperwork bills The End because The End was champion when it was written — the division rankings of 2 May 2002 and the Ikusa IV card of 4 June 2002 both predate the change — and its own champions page carries only the holder of the moment, in states that begin in January 2003. His own PURE roster card is the one document that reads against the reign: its title-history field gives "None as of yet" and its award field is blank. The show's own script and its own ring announcer carry the change, and The End gave his own account of it backstage the same night — "I am baffled myself on the loss…but more baffled on how I lost the belt." All of it stands as written. The reign ended when The End took the belt back in a fatal four-way, on a show the fed's own history calls Ikusa 6 and no surviving record dates.

reigns_index.h: 30 June 2002 · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Charlie Loc — Cruiserweight Championship won at Gold and Glory 2002 until 19 July 2002 Sources disagree — Fusion 82, 9 Jul 2002 — the Fusion strand bills The End the standing PCW Cruiserweight Champion and has him defend and retain against Brandi ("The End vs Brandi for the PCW Cruiserweight Championship"; he "walks out with the Cruiserweight strap around his waist"; "The blind jobber retains his cruiserweight title for another night", PCW's own results page for Fusion 82, 9 Jul 2002), four days after Fusion 81 gave him only the number one contendership. Turmoil 85 of 3 Jul 2002 and Fusion 83 of 19 Jul 2002 both bill Charlie Loc the champion, and Fusion 83 is where the belt actually changes. No match on either strand returns it. Both show records stand; the reigns here follow the strand the belt's own recorded changes run through. Fusion 81 and Fusion 82 are the same pair of shows the Extreme and Tag Team passes found billing standing champions against the rest of the fed's record. Gold and Glory 2002, 30 Jun 2002 — the page's own contradiction, read end to end, is a REPLAYED CLIP and not a second reading. The show carries a "Cruiserweight Championship history video package" immediately before the match; inside that package is the finish of Turmoil 81 of 28 May 2002 — "Winner and new PCW Cruiserweight Champion: Juan Borro / Dave: I can't believe it! Juan Borro has captured the PCW Cruiserweight title once again!" — followed by weeks of build narrated in the past tense ("A week later...", "Just last Tuesday...", "That Friday..."). The night's own match follows it: "The following match is scheduled for one fall and is 3 way TLC show down for the PCW CRUISERWEIGHT TITLE", with Borro billed "the Current PCW CRUISERWEIGHT CHAMPION" going in, and it ends on Charlie Loc — "HE'S DONE IT~! WE HAVE A NEW CRUISER WEIGHT CHAMPION~!" and "CHARLIE IS FINALLY THE PCW CRUISER WEIGHT CHAMPION!" (PCW's own results page for Gold and Glory 2002, 30 Jun 2002). The fed's own title log is right, Turmoil 85 of 3 Jul corroborates it, and the contradicting line is the previous title change replayed. No conflict is filed (the replay-document model, the museum's own rule). Fusion 81, 5 Jul 2002 — a NUMBER ONE CONTENDERSHIP match, not a title match. The show announces it twice in its own voice: "the next match is scheduled for one fall and is for the Number One Contendership to the Cruiserweight Title!" (PCW's own results page for Fusion 81, 5 Jul 2002, which also carries the whole match twice, the duplication its sibling pages carry). The fed's own log files it as a change from Charlie Loc to The End; Charlie Loc is billed "the PCW Cruiser Weight Champion" two days earlier on PCW's own results page for Turmoil 85, 3 Jul 2002 and again a fortnight later on PCW's own results page for Fusion 83, 19 Jul 2002, where he loses the belt for real. The stored champion-after is corrected. Turmoil 86, 9 Jul 2002 — another promotion's belt, filed under PCW's Cruiserweight Championship in the fed's own title log: the match's own text crowns "NEW PURE JUNIOR HEAVYWEIGHT CHAMPION, THE END!!" No correction row is filed, the standing shape for a row wanting a belt PCW's own title list does not hold (the RUSH Network Championship rows are the precedent).

Wrestling (2002)Joey Malone — Bantam Championship won at Pressure Point 19 until 29 September 2002 PRE-HISTORY, 2002-03-31 ('Resentment' special): another match missing from the title log, 'Bantam Championship: Matt Remicho vs. Areumna'derin Rahl,' a ladder match Remicho wins on-screen. But this predates the Bantam belt's real creation by over three months, and the show's own follow-up segment (billed 'B Championship?') has owner Reed Young announce beforehand that the title 'will still go on the line' despite the media's doubts, then AFTER Remicho wins, Young comes out and says 'it's way too soon to bring out the B Title... so I'm pulling it back' -- Remicho then lays Young out with the belt he never legitimately holds. Filed here as a note on the title, not a reign row. PCW's own results page for Turmoil 88, 23 Jul 2002 names the champion twice and it is DarkStar alone: "Clyde, the PCW Continental Champion Darkstar, and Syko the Goblin flank Nelson from left to right respectively. All three have sinister smirks on their faces, Darkstar with the Continental Title draped over his shoulder", and "OUR VERY OWN DUKE WILLIAMS WILL STEP INTO THE PROVERBIAL KILLING FIELDS AS HE TAKES ON NOT ONLY THE CONTINENTAL CHAMPION IN DARKSTAR, BUT THE DEMON KNOWN AS CLYDE TOO!!!!" The match’s own finish — "Winners: Clyde & DarkStar" — is a tag result the earlier passes read as a crowning. The fed’s own log was right all along and stores DarkStar (629) on BOTH sides of this row and of Fusion 86’s; NO CORRECTION IS OWED. Five further pages carry him as the standing champion across the whole stretch: PCW's own results page for Wrestle Vessel 2002, 28 Jul 2002 ("PCW Continental Champion Darkstar" in its own champions’ roll-call; "he comes to the ring wearing the fruits of his labor, the PCW Continental Championship... DARKSTAR!"; "by special order of Tyler Nelson, this will be a no-disqualification Continental Title match!"; "Darkstar retains the Continental Title with another huge pin over Legend, Inc!!"), PCW's own results page for Turmoil 89, 31 Jul 2002 ("the PCW Continental Champion Darkstar"), PCW's own results page for Turmoil 90, 6 Aug 2002 (El Diablo made "the #1 contender to the PCW Continental Championship"), PCW's own results page for Fusion 85, 9 Aug 2002 ("CLYDE AND THE PCW CONTINENTAL CHAMPION DARKSTAR!!!") and PCW's own results page for Fusion 86, 16 Aug 2002 (a defence against Rent-A-Villain). Wrestle Vessel 2002’s defence is a Continental title match the fed’s own title log carries no row for.

reigns_index.h: 6 August 2002 · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Violence Jack — Extreme Championship won at Turmoil 90 until 28 August 2002 Turmoil 90, 6 Aug 2002 — the card reads "Duzza and Mark Makonie vs Violence Jack and Flaymin Aymin (Extreme Championship)" and the show announces its own stipulation ("Duke: Right there hoss... Whoever pins the Champ walks with the belt!"). Violence Jack takes the fall ("Ibe Black can count as slow as he wants to, but Makonie is down for the count. 1... 2... 3!") and the fed's own broadcast calls the outcome in the next breath — "Dave: I don't think I can take much more of Violence Jack being Extreme Champion." PCW's own results page for Turmoil 90, 6 Aug 2002. The fed's own title log stores Flaymin Aymin on both sides and then stores Violence Jack as the champion AFTER Fusion 86 ten days later, on a night its own page calls him "STILL PCW extreme champion" — which is how the misplacement was visible at all. Fusion 86, 16 Aug 2002 — a defence, not the change: "Clay: Here is your winning of the match and STILL PCW extreme champion…VIOLENCEEEEE JACK!" PCW's own results page for Fusion 86, 16 Aug 2002. The fed's own log records the change here because it stores Flaymin Aymin as the champion going in; the belt had moved ten days earlier at Turmoil 90.

reigns_index.s: network championship | rush (2002) | g.o.d |  | g.o.d.
reigns_index.h: 18 August 2002 · RUSH (2002)G.O.D. — Network Championship won at Crossroads 2002 until 12 September 2002 Sources disagree. The fed's own written summary of the change and its Title History page both date it "on 9/5/2002 at Adrenaline 16", and the fed's own booking record puts Adrenaline 16 on 12 Sep 2002 (5 Sep 2002 is Adrenaline 15). Both readings stand. The change is dated 12 Sep 2002, because the title match is on the card of Adrenaline 16 (Livewire, Tyronne Sharper and G.O.D. in a triple threat, won by Livewire) and the page's line names the right show and the wrong day, or the right day and the wrong show, and cannot be both. No length is given for this reign or for the next, because of the disagreement. One defence is on a held card, not in the fed's own title log: Adrenaline 14 (29 Aug 2002), announced "for the RUSH Network Championship"; he beat Livewire by pinfall, the man who would take the belt from him a fortnight later.

reigns_index.s: syndicate championship | rush (2002) | danny ferguson |  | el spiffy!
reigns_index.h: 18 August 2002 · RUSH (2002)El Spiffy! — Syndicate Championship won at Crossroads 2002 until 2002-12-01 (circa) Five defences are on held cards, none in the fed's own title log, each announced as a Syndicate title match: Adrenaline 14 (29 Aug 2002; he lost the match and kept the belt, the ring announcer's words being "Your winner, due to interference, Scott Cage! But still the Syndicate Champion, El Spiffy!"), Adrenaline 15 (5 Sep 2002, beat Wes Outlett), Adrenaline 16 (12 Sep 2002, beat Chris Matthews), Adrenaline 17 (19 Sep 2002, a four-way over Chris Matthews, The Masked Mullet and Caleb McGlocklan) and Adrenaline 19 (4 Oct 2002, retained when Stimpo was disqualified). The belt itself was stolen twice and the championship never moved: Stimpo impersonated him to hand himself the belt on Adrenaline 18, the CEO Rush Mason took it back and voided it on screen ("it's a good thing you were just joking about that whole 'giving the belt away' thing... So why don't you just keep this belt for now"), the real El Spiffy! was found tied up backstage, and Stimpo laid him out and took the belt again on Adrenaline 19. A sixth defence is the WCW Hardcore match at Rising From the Ashes (13 Oct 2002), booked on the card of Adrenaline 19 (he challenges Stimpo "to a match at the Pay-Per-View! For HIS Spiffy-cate title"); the fed's own pay-per-view script, served as a document, has Sheila Tyrone announce "here is your winner, and STILL RUSH Wrestling Syndicate Champion, EL SPIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIFFYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYY" and James Williams say he returned "JUST A DAY AFTER BEING HOSPITALIZED FOR A BACK INJURY" to defend it. The reign ended after the fed's own record, which carries no later Syndicate change and whose title list (about October 2002) still names him champion: the PCW card of Turmoil 102 (3 Dec 2002) has Stimpo "winning his first title, the Syndicate Title on Sunday Adrenaline defeating both Ebola III and Spiffy! in their triple threat match" (the Adrenaline of Sunday 1 Dec 2002, on no capture), and Decimation 2002's commentary says "Even when he lost his belt, Stimpo pinned Ebola in the triple threat to end it!" and that he held "the belt for 107 days"; 18 Aug to 1 Dec 2002 is 105 days; the commentary's count and the calendar differ, and no length is claimed.

reigns_index.h: 29 August 2002 · RUSH (2002)Brock Newbludd — World Championship won at Adrenaline 14 until 18 October 2002 Two defences are on record that the fed's own title log does not carry. First, the card of Adrenaline 16 (12 Sep 2002): he beat Tyler Valentine by pinfall in a match Sheila Tyrone introduces as "for the RUSH WORLD HEAVYWEIGHT TITLE", and the next show's recap segment names it too. Second, on a show with no card on file: the fed's own news post of 13 Oct 2002 says "Brock Newbludd defended his World Title against Tyler Valentine and Chris Matthews" at Rising From the Ashes. The fed's own news post of 21 Oct calls Newbludd "the 3rd ex-RUSH champ", which is what this chain makes him. The fed's own title log ends with the vacancy: the fed's own news post of 20 Oct has a World Title tournament "underway this week on Adrenaline 22" with its final booked for RUSH's December pay-per-view, and the fed's own title list names no later World champion. The card of Decimation 2002 (22 Dec 2002), the December pay-per-view PCW and RUSH staged together, has the match for the vacant title, and Tyler Valentine won it; the title log and the card disagree, and both are recorded (#sources-disagree).

The reign did not end in a match: the fed's own World title history as captured on 25 Dec 2005 says Toxic "would be the first and only XW world champion as the company closed, ending the GCW title's history", and ACWF VI (6 Apr 2005), the six-man match that crowned the next champion, was billed "poised to crown a new GCW World Heavyweight Champion" without him in it ("Toxic wants a shot to regain the world title"). reigns_index.h: 12 September 2002 · RUSH (2002)Livewire — Network Championship won at Adrenaline 16 until 2002-12-10 (circa) Sources disagree. The fed's own written summary of the change and its Title History page both date it "on 9/5/2002 at Adrenaline 16", and the fed's own booking record puts Adrenaline 16 on 12 Sep 2002 (5 Sep 2002 is Adrenaline 15). Both readings stand. The change is dated 12 Sep 2002, because the title match is on the card of Adrenaline 16 and the page's line names the right show and the wrong day, or the right day and the wrong show, and cannot be both. No length is given for the previous reign or this one's start, because of the disagreement. Two defences are on record, neither in the fed's own title log. First, Adrenaline 18 (27 Sep 2002), announced "for the RUSH NETWORK TITLE": the billed challenger Stimpo never appeared and Joe Bananas attacked the champion instead; the card gives no result and none is claimed, and the belt did not change hands. Second, Rising From the Ashes (13 Oct 2002; the fed's own pay-per-view script, served as a document): Sheila Tyrone announces "the RUSH Network Title", Livewire beats Joe Bananas with the Electricity ("Winner: Livewire", "LIVEWIRE KEEPS THE NETWORK TITLE!"), and the fed's own newsdesk has it in Bananas's own words, "Ah lost ta Livewire at Rising From the Ashes". The reign ended after the fed's own record: the fed's own title log carries no later Network change and its own title list (about October 2002) still names him champion, but the PCW card of Fusion 101 (20 Dec 2002) has Matt Hunt walk out with "his newly acquired Network Title", saying he won it "last week on Turmoil", and the commentary calls Livewire "past his prime" (reign r005); how Livewire lost it is on no served card.

reigns_index.h: between 2002-09-13 and 2002-09-17 (circa) · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Syko the Goblin — Television Championship until 6 October 2002 The change falls between 13 and 17 Sep 2002: Turmoil 96 of 17 Sep 2002 has the belt back on Syko the Goblin in his own words, a week before the Turmoil 97 billing. PCW ran no show at all between Fusion 90 of 13 Sep and Turmoil 96 of 17 Sep 2002 (its own booking record), so the change falls in a gap the fed staged nothing in — the FED-SCHEDULE bracket shape. Fusion 90's own page carries the oddity beside it: after Rush Mason wins the title match, Venneman Pendragon "begins to stalk after the pleading Goblin, his eyes focused on his prize, the TV Title" — Syko is carrying the physical belt on the night he is recorded losing it. The change itself is in no surviving PCW page; the date is the bracket the fed's own record supports.

reigns_index.h: 17 September 2002 · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Anarchy — Cruiserweight Championship won at Turmoil 96 until 6 October 2002 Turmoil 96, 17 Sep 2002 — the fed MERGED THE RISING STAR CHAMPIONSHIP INTO THIS BELT on this night, and says so in its own voice: "the Cruiserweight and Rising Star titles are merged", "This is the last match ever where the Rising Star title will be seen", and the match "will crown the undisputed Primetime Championship Wrestling Cruiserweight Champion" (PCW's own results page for Turmoil 96, 17 Sep 2002). Anarchy carried the Rising Star belt in and Brandi the Cruiserweight belt; Anarchy left with one belt. The fed's own title log records Anarchy as champion on both sides of the match and carries no row for the merge. PCW revived the Rising Star Championship four months later (Shanghaied 2003 of 26 Jan 2003 crowns "the first Rising Star Champion in a very long time"; Fusion 108 of 7 Feb 2003 calls it "the newly revived Rising Star division"), so the merge records a dated event, not a permanent state.

Kennedy pinned Asa Fountain in the chain match, the Dead Presidents were handed the Tag Team titles, and the masks came off: Kennedy was William S. Powell, Nixon was Reginald V. Lovecraft, and the masked man at ringside was their campaign manager, Roger Schultz. The ring announcer called the team the new FSW Tag Team Champions, Politically Incorrect. Defences on record. Glory 16, 30 October 2002: Magnum Wolf pulled the referee out of the ring at the count of two, and Politically Incorrect kept the Tag Team titles. Glory 17, 6 November 2002: The bell rang before the referee's count of three on Politically Incorrect, and the timekeeper ruled them the winners and still Tag Team Champions on the 20-minute time limit. Glory 18, 13 November 2002: Roger Schultz hit the referee with a tag title belt, and Jesse Ramey and John Jupiter won by disqualification, but Politically Incorrect kept the Tag Team titles.

THE BRACKET IS A FED-SCHEDULE FACT, not a capture gap, and it is the SAME gap that hides The H.I.T.'s second Television reign: PCW held no show at all between Fusion 97 of 1 Nov 2002 and Alliances 2002 of 24 Nov 2002 (PCW's own booking record carries four bookings in November — Fusion 97, Alliances 2002, Turmoil 101 and Fusion 98), and Alliances 2002 names no Extreme champion at all. Fusion 97 of 1 Nov 2002 frames Venneman Pendragon as "the Television and Extreme Champion"; BOTH of his belts changed hands inside those three empty weeks. reigns_index.s: cruiserweight championship | pcw (primetime, 2000–2004) | tim walden |  | tim walden
reigns_index.h: 24 November 2002 · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Tim Walden — Cruiserweight Championship won at Alliances 2002 until 7 January 2003 Alliances 2002, 24 Nov 2002 — the card bills "Tim Walden (c) vs The H.I.T" and the fed's own log records Walden champion on both sides, but the page crowns him: "WINNER...AND NEW PCW CRUISERWEIGHT CHAMPION....TIM WALDEN!!!". Cyclonica was the champion going in. Fusion 100, 13 Dec 2002 — a NUMBER ONE CONTENDER'S match, not a title match: "Winner and NEW #1 Contender To The Cruiserweight Title: Teresa Tomas" (PCW's own results page for Fusion 100, 13 Dec 2002). Decimation 2002 of 22 Dec ("STILL CRUISERWEIGHT CHAMPION, TIM WALDEN!!!!!!!") and Turmoil 106 of 31 Dec ("winner...and STILL Cruiserweight Champion....TIM WALDEN!") both keep the belt on Walden. Teresa Tomas never held it. Decimation 2002, 22 Dec 2002 — ANOTHER PROMOTION'S BELT, filed under PCW's Cruiserweight Championship in the fed's own title log. The El Romantico / Vilas Lavagna match is announced on the page itself: "Ladies and Gentlemen this match has been changed and is now NO DQ for the PURE JUNIOR HEAVYWEIGHT TITLE OF THE WORLD!", with the commentary adding "How can they do this, PCW is a total different promotion from PURE" (PCW's own results page for Decimation 2002, 22 Dec 2002). No correction row is filed: PCW's own title list holds no id for PURE's belt, the standing shape the RUSH Network Championship rows and Turmoil 86 of 9 Jul 2002 already sit in. The same show has Tim Walden retain the Cruiserweight Championship in a different match. The reign ends by the fed taking the belt off its holder, not in a match. Turmoil 107 of 7 Jan 2003 ends in a draw — both men's shoulders down — and Clay announces it: "...AND AS A RESULT OF THE DRAW..... PRESIDENT DUKE WILLIAMS IS REMOVING THE TITLE FROM TIM WALDEN AND SUSPENDING IT UNTIL SHANGHAIED WHERE TIM WALDEN WILL HAVE TO FACE EL ROMANTICO ONCE AGAIN FOR THE BELT!!!" (PCW's own results page for Turmoil 107, 7 Jan 2003). The fed's word for the act is removing it from him. The belt is then vacant to Shanghaied 2003. Tim Walden's reign is one unbroken run, 24 Nov 2002 – 7 Jan 2003.

THE CONTINENTAL CHAMPIONSHIP AND KNEELS BEFORE HIM!!!", and The Chef begins to "knight" him before cracking him over the head with the rolling pin) and the match's own stipulation — crowned by the Chef — is satisfied by nobody. Only the belt's final holder on the night is carried.

reigns_index.h: 22 December 2002 · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Totally Tubular Tommy — Continental Championship won at Decimation 2002 until 16 March 2003 Decimation 2002, 22 Dec 2002 — the Treble Jeopardy Match for the PCW Continental Championship; the fed's own card bills "Rush Mason (c)" and its own page announces him "THE PCW CONTINENTAL CHAMPION" going in. Fusion 102, 27 Dec 2002 — a NON-TITLE match, in the fed’s own words. PCW's own results page for Fusion 102, 27 Dec 2002 ends "Winner: Chet King" and the broadcast says immediately: "Dave: This wasn’t for the title but ya gotta think he just proved he’s worthy of a shot." The same page bills Totally Tubular Tommy walking out "with the Continental Title around his waist" as "the new Continental Champion after that Treble Jeopardy Match at Decimation", and PCW's own results page for Shanghaied 2003, 26 Jan 2003 ends "WINNER, AND STILL CONTINENTAL CHAMPION, TOTALLY TUBULAR TOMMY!". Chet King never held the belt; Tommy’s reign runs unbroken. Turmoil 116, 11 Mar 2003 — a main event with no title on the line. PCW's own results page for Turmoil 116, 11 Mar 2003 announces it as "This contest is scheduled for one fall!" with no championship stipulation (compare the same fed’s "and is for the PCW CONTINENTAL CHAMPIONSHIP" wording elsewhere), and no "new champion" call follows the finish; five days later the March Madness 2003 card still bills "Totally Tubular Tommy (c)". The log stores Pharaoh, per the fed's own roster, as champion-after, but the man who won is Titu Xansiv — whom this same page bills "Titu Xansiv - THE PHARAOH!" — and he is not that roster entry. Pharaoh never held the belt.

reigns_index.s: world championship | rush (2002) | tyler valentine |  | tyler valentine
reigns_index.h: 22 December 2002 · RUSH (2002)Tyler Valentine — World Championship won at Decimation 2002 end unknown The fed's own title log and the cards disagree, and both are recorded (#sources-disagree). The fed's own title log stops at the vacancy of 18 October 2002 and its own title list names no World champion after Brock Newbludd. The pay-per-view card of Decimation 2002, staged by PCW and RUSH together, has the match for the vacant title: the announcer's introduction above, the commentary "Two and a half months without a champion and we're finally going to have our rightful leader!", Tyler Valentine beating McGlocklan, and the announcer's closing call. The cards that follow bill him champion. Fusion 103 (3 Jan 2003) stages "Tyler Valentine's RUSH World Championship coronation" and introduces him as "the RUSH World Champion"; Turmoil 107 (7 Jan 2003) introduces him as "the RUSH World Heavyweight Champion"; Shanghaied III (26 Jan 2003) bills "Tyler Valentine (c) vs Marvin Harris" for the RUSH World title, the announcer introduces him as "the RUSH World Heavyweight Champion", and the match ends with the announcer's "YOUR WINNER, AND STILL RUSH WORLD HEAVYWEIGHT CHAM—" cut off by Valentine, who finishes the call himself. No card on file shows the belt leaving him: none of the PCW cards on file dated after Shanghaied III (the Turmoil and Fusion cards of 28 Jan 2003 onward, March Madness, Spring Fling and Supremacy 2003, Shanghaied IV and the Turmoil cards to 17 Apr 2004) names him or the RUSH World title, so the reign carries no end date and none is claimed.

reigns_index.h: 2002 (circa) · PTC (2002)(unresolved — a second Global Title Tourney) — PTC Global Championship end unknown (Referenced in alliance news; its winner is not named in the captured fragments) Mid-2002. CONTRADICTED BY THE EVENT'S OWN TEXT: the I-PPV site's own front page has the belt homeless from the Nosferatu/Phoenix final until 20 April 2003 — "for the first time since... the PTC Global Title will finally find a home" — which leaves no room for a second tournament to have crowned anyone in mid-2002. The alliance news engine's own reference to that second tourney stands as recorded; so does the I-PPV's account. Neither is picked, and the two-tournament shape may yet reconcile them if the second tourney turns out to have been announced and never finished. TIER-3: PTCpedia's own fuller title history names no second Global Title Tourney at all in this window — instead it has Obsidian winning the belt in a title MATCH (not a tournament) at "Night of Champions," 19 May 2002. Whether Obsidian's win is what the alliance news engine's own "second Global Title Tourney" reference garbled, or the two are genuinely different, unrecovered events, is not resolved here — both stand. PTCpedia's own PTC Global Title article (/promotions/ptc/archive/ptcpedia-ptc-global-title.html, captured 19 Aug 2010) — a fuller, later-compiled title history than the alliance news engine's own partial lineage; per docs/PROCESS.md's hub rule, its claims corroborate the existing record rather than override it.

Axtell's own partner, Jimmy Nguyen, blinded him with cologne passed in by Chandler Tsonda, letting Penance recover to finish him. PWC TV, 22 March 2003: Penance retained the PWC Tag Team Championship, eliminating all three challenging teams in a gauntlet match: pinning Sammy Bello of Special Delivery with the Ideological Crucifixion, chokebombing Scourge of Total Violation, and finishing with a tombstone piledriver on Gunner Gojoh of the Deathmatch Samurai.

reigns_index.h: 30 April 2003 · PCW (Primetime, 2000–2004)Miss Moonlight — Cruiserweight Championship won at Turmoil 123 end unknown Fusion 120, 2 May 2003 — the four corners match is announced for the belt and Flaymin Aymin pins the champion to win it, but NO CHAMPIONSHIP CALL FOLLOWS: the page ends "Clay: Your winner...Flaymin Aymin!" and nothing more (PCW's own results page for Fusion 120, 2 May 2003). The fed's own title log records no change, and Miss Moonlight is billed "the current Cruiserweight Champion" on the next show a week later (PCW's own results page for Fusion 121, 9 May 2003, where she retains) and every show after it. Aymin is billed champion nowhere. His reign is retired and hers runs unbroken. Turmoil 130, 19 Jun 2003 — SOCIETY never won the Cruiserweight Championship, he STOLE it. He walks out "wearing the PCW Cruiserweight Title around his neck", says "Many of you are wondering why I took this piece of property away from Miss Moonlight", and declares: "since I now own this belt, I HEREBY DECLARE MYSELF THE PCW CRUISERWEIGHT CHAMPION!!" The broadcast never accepts it — "He's destroyed TWO PCW officials, and stolen the PCW Cruiserweight Title!" — and calls Miss Moonlight the Cruiserweight Champion inside the same match (PCW's own results page for Turmoil 130, 19 Jun 2003). The finish is a disqualification besides. The card's "(c)" sits on Tessa Windsor-Green, PCW's Television Champion, who held this belt at no point. Turmoil 131, 25 Jun 2003 — the fed settles it in its own voice with Miss Moonlight refereeing SOCIETY's self-declared defence: "Jeff:...the PCW Cruiserweight Title's on the line, so let's get this match started! / Dave:...You know that Miss Moonlight's the champion." She demands the belt from SOCIETY and "begrudgingly, SOCIETY hands it over", raises it to the crowd and gives it to the timekeeper; the match is then thrown out ("THE RESULT OF THIS MATCH, WHEN MISS MOONLIGHT WAKES UP, IS A NO CONTEST!") (PCW's own results page for Turmoil 131, 25 Jun 2003). No reign is filed for SOCIETY. PCW closed for roughly six months between Turmoil 131 of 25 Jun 2003 and Turmoil 132 of 21 Dec 2003, and THIS BELT CROSSED THE GAP ON ITS CHAMPION. Turmoil 137 of 7 Feb 2004 stages her return with the belt still on her: "the PCW CRUISERWEIGHT TITLE AROUND HER WAIST!!" and "Dave: It's MISS MOONLIGHT!! THE LAST PCW CRUISERWEIGHT CHAMPION BEFORE THE COMPANY CLOSED!!", the same page billing her "the PCW Cruiserweight champion, Naomi Kawaii" and titling the segment "The Mega Soaring Arrows reveal Naomi Kawaii as the former PCW Cruiserweight Champion Miss Moonlight" (PCW's own results page for Turmoil 137, 7 Feb 2004). Turmoil 138 of 14 Feb 2004 says it again — the Cruiserweight title's own name plate reads MISS MOONLIGHT beside "the woman formerly known as Miss Moonlight", and the backstage interview corrects itself from "the reigning PCW Cruiserweight champion, Miss Moonlight—" to "reigning PCW Cruiserweight champion, NAOMI KAWAII" (PCW's own results page for Turmoil 138, 14 Feb 2004); she retains on that show, the belt's last surviving defence. The reign is one run under two billed names (Miss Moonlight, then Naomi Kawaii, per the fed's own roster); the holder is carried under the billing the reign began with.
